issues.title: AMD RX 9060 XT (RDNA 4 / DCN 4.0.1): flip_done timed out during simpledrm→amdgpu framebuffer handoff on boot. UPDATE: cause identified
issues.author: Sebastian Rosende
issues.description:
### Description

On every boot with an AMD RX 9060 XT connected via DisplayPort, the system fails to transition from the `simpledrm` framebuffer (early boot) to the `amdgpu` DRM driver. The failure is in `amdgpu_dm_commit_planes` during the `drm_fb_helper_set_par` modeset commit, triggered by `kworker` approximately 16 seconds into boot. This results in a cascade of `flip_done timed out` errors spanning approximately 3 minutes, a black screen, and no display output for the remainder of the session.

I first experienced this when upgrading to Bazzite 44. Then reproduced it booting a liveusb of Aurora. At first I thought it was a kwin issue ([reported and fixed upstream](https://invent.kde.org/plasma/plasma-login-manager/-/merge_requests/130)) but apparently it crashes even before kwin, and it keeps crashing even after updating to a version that includes that fix.

Had to rollback to Bazzite 43.20260420.

### Observed Result

Black screen. No display output after early boot. `flip_done timed out` cascading errors in dmesg.

### Expected Result

Normal desktop display output.

| GPU | AMD Radeon RX 9060 XT (Navi 44, RDNA 4) — PCI 0x1002:0x7590, rev c0 |

## Brief summary of the problem:

When decoding YouTube AV1 2160p60 through VA-API (Mesa radeonsi) in Firefox, the VCN clock stays at roughly 800–1200 MHz (max 2934 MHz) with `power_dpm_force_performance_level=auto`. Average decode latency is fine (<1 ms per frame as measured by Firefox), but about every 30 frames one frame takes 20–55 ms, which is more than the 16.68 ms frame budget. Firefox then decides HW decoding is slow and recreates the decoder, which shows up as visible stutter about every 10 s. It is 100% reproducible. Firefox side: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2073923

Pinning only the VCN clocks makes the problem go away:

```
echo manual > /sys/class/drm/card1/device/power_dpm_force_performance_level
echo 2 > /sys/class/drm/card1/device/pp_dpm_vclk
echo 2 > /sys/class/drm/card1/device/pp_dpm_dclk
```

| DPM setting | vclk during playback | frames > 16.68 ms |
|---|---|---|
| auto | ~800–1200 MHz, fluctuating; sclk dips to 27–43 MHz | 16 in ~10 s (spikes up to 55 ms) |
| high | 2934 MHz | 9 in ~2 min (max 24 ms) |
| manual, vclk/dclk level 2 | 2934 MHz / 2200 MHz | 8 in ~100 s (max 22 ms) |

issues.title: amdgpu-dkms installation failure can leave driver blacklisted
issues.author: Ben Hutchings
issues.description:
The postinst script of amdgpu-dkms includes:

```sh
			echo "blacklist amdgpu" >/etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-amdgpu.conf
			"$POSTINST" "$NAME" "$CVERSION" "/usr/share/$PACKAGE_NAME" "$ARCH" "$2"
			rc=$?
			rm -f /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-amdgpu.conf
```

This is trying to ensure that `blacklist-amdgpu.conf` always gets cleaned
up, but:

1. This script starts with `set -e`, so if the `"$POSTINST"` script fails
then this script exits immediately.
2. If the system loses power or crashes while `"$POSTINST"` is running,
there is nothing to clean up the file.

This is not just a theoretical problem - Debian has received multiple bug
reports that appear to be caused by this:
[#1094206](https://bugs.debian.org/1094206),
[#1094767](https://bugs.debian.org/1094767),
[#1101203](https://bugs.debian.org/1101203).

Something like this should fix these problems:

```sh
			mkdir -p /run/modprobe.d
			echo "blacklist amdgpu" >/run/modprobe.d/blacklist-amdgpu.conf
			rc=0
			"$POSTINST" "$NAME" "$CVERSION" "/usr/share/$PACKAGE_NAME" "$ARCH" "$2" || rc=$?
			rm -f /run/modprobe.d/blacklist-amdgpu.conf
```

but I haven't tested it.

**Time-oriented Execution Flow & Root Cause** The issue stems from a missing sandbox isolation wrapper, which causes a sequential state contamination when combined with the Kbuild toolchain.

5. **False Positive**: `objtool` runs, validates the _stale_ `conftest.o` left by step 1, and returns `0`. `AC_KERNEL_COMPILE_IFELSE` catches this `0` and incorrectly defines `HAVE_DRM_MODE_C

```
amdgpu 0000:0b:00.0: [drm] *ERROR* Unsupported screen format RA24 little-endian (0x34324152)

issues.title: Display pipeline stall on memory clock speed change with FAMS2 on gfx1201
issues.author: fililip
issues.description:
## Brief summary of the problem:

With high enough display bandwidth requirements to trigger SubVP or DRR SubVP reclocking, memory clock P-state changes (automatic or manual DPM) cause the desktop to stall for a few frames, causing a very visible short freeze, which is unlikely to be desired during reclocking.

This turns out to be a faulty hardware lock introduced in https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/agd5f/linux/-/commit/00c391102abc13763e2bfc90e05503109b19f074, later renamed in https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/agd5f/linux/-/commit/6d92c4d03063480a60bbc3ff61d22197c931f411.

Working around this lock by either removing it entirely or gating it behind a `dmub_hw_lock_mgr_does_context_require_lock` check works flawlessly and eliminates the stall completely: [fams2-mclk-stutter-workaround-minimal.patch](/uploads/09e73a73cacf4c580c8835aceaa574ee/fams2-mclk-stutter-workaround-minimal.patch). I tested this workaround on various different configurations (HDR, VRR, MPO, suspend/resume, hotplugs, etc.) and it never caused any issues. Perhaps it's not needed for dGPUs at all? Especially since without it, SubVP looks like it's doing the correct thing - hiding the clock switch perfectly without any hitches.

Other people report temporary screen blanking rather than stutter on a clock speed change, but it turns out that's due to DRR on some Samsung panels, which seem to blank on VRR on/off transitions. This can be worked around by always setting the `VRR_ENABLED` property to `1` on affected CRT

issues.title: drm/radeon: fence waiters hang indefinitely after commit 5f08eee9c3fb (wake event stealing)
issues.description:
## Summary

After commit 5f08eee9c3fb ("drm/radeon: restore hardware polling in fence_is_signaled to fix performance regression"), screen freezes occur on Radeon HD 5450 (Cedar) under heavy 2D redraw load.

This is the exact "wake event stealing" issue flagged by Sashiko AI during the patch review: https://lists.freedesktop.org/archives/dri-devel/2026-July/585290.html

## Symptoms

- Screen freezes during fast redraw (fast feh slideshow)
- Mouse cursor still moves, keyboard works
- Switching to TTY and back recovers the screen
- Launching hardware-accelerated `glxgears` recovers the screen
- `dmesg` is empty, no GPU errors
- All Xorg threads in `S (sleeping)`: `Xorg:rcs0` and `Xorg:disk$0` stuck in `futex_wait`

## Environment

- GPU: Radeon HD 5450 (Cedar)
- OS: Debian testing/unstable
- Kernel: 7.2.8+deb14-amd64 (regression introduced in 7.1.10)
- Xorg with glamor, DRI 3, TearFree on

## Root cause analysis

`radeon_fence_is_signaled()` calls `radeon_fence_activity()` which updates `last_seq` but does NOT call `wake_up_all()`. When a GPU interrupt is subsequently missed (common on older Cedar hardware), `radeon_fence_process()` sees `seq == last_seq` (already advanced), returns false, and skips `wake_up_all()`. The sleeping thread is never woken.

## Proposed fix

Schedule a workqueue item that calls `wake_up_all()` unconditionally when `radeon_fence_activity()` detects new completions. This restores the stolen wake event while avoiding the deadlock and PREEMPT_RT issues.

issues.author: Rauf Gungor
issues.description:
Building  Linux 7.2 kernel on Fedora 44 with RDNA 3 (RX 7800 XT) or RDNA 4 (RX 9070 XT) graphics cards (two other, RX9060XT and RX9070 are working fine) and experiencing black screen when KDE Plasma / Wayland attempts to initialize (while TTY/Ctrl+Alt+F2 still works), I found the root cause and a hardware workaround.

The Symptom/Log:\
The kernel shows infinite timing controller loops right before the freeze:\
“amdgpu 0000:03:00.0: \[drm\] REG_WAIT timeout 1us \* 150000 tries - optc401_disable_crtc”\
Followed by:\
“workqueue: name exceeds WQ_NAME_LEN. Truncating to: hdmi_frl_status_polling_workque”

The Cause:\
The Linux 7.2 amdgpu module features a severe link-training race condition loop inside its newly rewritten HDMI 2.1 Fixed Rate Link (FRL) status polling workqueue engine when encountering certain monitor HDR metadata profiles. The Output Timing Generator (OTG) gets permanently stuck in a busy loop, locking out Plasma Login Manager Wayland .

The Fix/Workaround:\
Do not use a native HDMI-to-HDMI cable. Instead, use a DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter (or a native DisplayPort cable) connected directly to the GPU’s DisplayPort output.

By forcing the signal through the DisplayPort protocol pipeline, the driver completely skips the buggy native HDMI FRL polling engine, allowing the display timing registers to pass immediately without hitting the 150k register stall loop. Everything logs in cleanly with HDR functional.

## Brief summary of the problem:

amdgpu's Display Core supports the DRM EDID override layer (`drm.edid_firmware` / `edid_override`), but only consults it when it is _not_ doing its own hardware read. When it detects a present sink it reads the EDID over the wire (via `dm_helpers_read_local_edid`), and if that read returns `EDID_NO_RESPONSE` (logged as `EDID err: 2`) it synthesises a fallback mode rather than falling back to the override configured by the user. **Respect the configured EDID override whenever it is set.** When a user has configured `drm.edid_firmware=<conn>:<file>` or a debugfs `edid_override`, DC should serve it and skip the hardware read. When a game or graphic program doesn't fully load the GPU (e.g. due to CPU/memory bottleneck or a frame rate cap) the amdgpu driver increases the core clock frequency way too much just to keep GPU load at around 70%. This results in a way higher power consumption for no increase in frame rate.

As an example with my RX 9070, the game No Rest For The Wicked capped at 110 fps uses 220 W because the driver tries to get to 70% GPU load by increasing clocks to almost 3000 MHz. Manually setting the power limit at 130 W causes the clocks to drop to 1800 MHz while the frame rate stays the same.

This happens in any game or graphic program that loads the GPU significantly but not at 100%. It's not limited to any particular game. The default GPU load targeting of 70% seems to be way too low, at least for the RX 9070 (XT). A default GPU load target of 100% probably isn't optimal for latency, but 90-95% will lower power usage a lot without increasing latency.

## Brief summary of the problem:

On a Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 14APU8 (Ryzen 7 7840S), every s2idle suspend returns by itself after 1–5 seconds and never reaches S0i3. I expect the system to stay suspended until I wake it (or until the RTC alarm, in the amd-s2idle test) and to reach hardware sleep.

## Brief description

On an ASUS Zenbook S16 (UM5606GA, Ryzen AI 9 465, Radeon 880M, DCN 3.5) with a Samsung ATNA60HR07-0 eDP OLED panel (2880x1800), every kernel in the 7.0.x/7.1.x series wedges the internal display at the moment the GDM Wayland greeter starts, on 100% of boots. Kernel 6.19.14 works.

issues.title: Hardware acceleration breaks YouTube/video playback on Ryzen 9950X iGPU due to default 512MB UMA Frame Buffer Size
issues.author: Patrick Martel
issues.description:
Environment:

- OS: Debian Forky
- Browser: Brave Browser (Chromium-based)
- Hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X with Integrated Radeon Graphics
- Kernel Driver: amdgpu

Problem:

With hardware acceleration enabled, YouTube fails to render properly giving artifacts. Current workarounds are disabling hardware acceleration and/or changing the ANGLE graphics backend.

Root Cause & Solution:

The issue stems from the motherboard's default BIOS configuration for "UMA Frame Buffer Size" being set to "Auto", which defaults the baseline dedicated VRAM to 512MB.

Manually changing the BIOS setting "UMA Frame Buffer Size" from "Auto" to "1GB" (or higher) and reverting all browser workarounds back to default completely resolves the issue for me.

Can others confirm?

issues.author: Curtis Vogt
issues.description:
## Summary

On a Navi 48 (RX 9070 XT) driving a 4K HDMI sink whose EDID advertises `Maximum TMDS clock: 300 MHz`, no HDMI Forum VSDB, and a **YCbCr 4:2:0 Video Data Block** listing 3840x2160@60 and 4096x2160@60, kernel 7.1.5 correctly selects **YCbCr 4:2:0** for 4K60 (297 MHz, within the sink limit).

Kernel 7.2.2 instead commits **RGB 4:4:4 @ 594 MHz** for the same mode (roughly double the advertised sink limit) and the display goes black. `create_validate_stream_for_sink()` walks color depth 16 -\> 14 -\> 12 -\> 10 -\> 8, prunes everything above 8 bpc with "Encoder validation failure", then commits RGB 8-bpc. **No YCbCr 4:2:0 stream is ever validated or committed**: every logged validation attempt and every committed stream is RGB, even though this mode is one the sink can accept _only_ as 4:2:0.

Net effect: black screen on boot as soon as the compositor sets 4K60. The machine is otherwise fully functional (session starts, reachable via TTY).

| 7.2.0-1-cachyos | (not captured) | \-- | black screen |
| 7.2.2-1-cachyos | RGB 4:4:4 | 594 MHz | black screen |
